source.title: Efficient Training of Self-Supervised Speech Foundation Models on a Compute Budget
source.authors: Andy T. Liu; Yi-Cheng Lin; Hai-Bin Wu; Stefan Winkler; Hung-Yi Lee

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: It studies scaling and compute-budget trade-offs in self-supervised speech foundation models, extending related scaling questions to speech. It does not reproduce language-model scaling-law fits.
record.gate_note: The paper varies model size at a fixed 1.33 × 10^18 FLOPS budget and reports training/validation loss and downstream metrics in Figure 2. It reports a validation-loss curve with an optimum near 200% of Slim and U-shaped performance curves. Table 3 reports downstream metrics for wav2vec 2.0 Slim at four data sizes under a fixed FLOPS budget. The prior speech scaling result in reference [30] is cited, not tested. Table 2’s architecture comparisons report downstream metrics, not held-out loss, so they do not test V4 as worded.
record.test_reason: The study trains speech self-supervised models (HuBERT, wav2vec 2.0, TERA), not language models. It fits no power law of any kind. Its results come from one fixed FLOPS budget (1.33e18): a model-size sweep showing a U-shaped train/valid loss and downstream curve with an optimum near 200% of Slim, a data-size sweep at fixed model and compute, and a Slim-vs-Small architecture comparison. None of this measures what a version names. V1, V2, V3, V4 and V6 concern language models. V5 needs the power-law form to hold in another modality, and no power law is fitted. V3 needs the optimum to grow as a power of compute, and only one budget is used. A U-shaped isoFLOP curve is what Hoffmann-style compute-optimal analysis expects, so it is not the curve 'bending away from a single power law' in V7. These results are related findings and are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that, under a compute budget, factors other than the SSL objective (architecture, data size, model size) drive speech SSL performance most. Narrower, deeper Slim models beat common 3-layer Small models at equal parameters and compute. Sufficient unique pretraining data matters more than repeated iteration. An optimal model size exists for a given FLOPS budget, about 200% of Slim in their setup.
record.recipe_differences: Speech self-supervised models and downstream speech benchmarks; fixed-budget sweeps rather than language-model held-out-loss power-law fitting across parameters, tokens, and compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper varies model architecture, model size, data size, and SSL objective. With data size changing at fixed FLOPS, performance falls notably below 100 hours; model-size performance has a U-shaped curve at the tested budget.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed 1.33e18 FLOPS budget, speech SSL models (HuBERT, wav2vec 2.0, TERA) show U-shaped train/valid loss and ASR/ASV curves over model size. The optimum is near 200% of Slim (~40M params); Base and Large underperform at that budget.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Speech SSL pretraining shows a compute-optimal model size at a fixed FLOPS budget (isoFLOP optimum), analogous to LM compute-optimal analyses (single budget only).

fits_no_version.finding: Across the fixed-compute model-size sweep, the authors report that pretraining loss, ASV EER and ASR WER 'show similar trends' for all three objectives. Figure only; no correlation coefficient is given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In speech SSL, downstream ASR/ASV performance tracks pretraining loss across model sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed compute and model (wav2vec 2.0 Slim), more unique pretraining data with fewer repeats improves most SUPERB metrics (ASR WER 39.60/23.88/18.66/17.01 for 1/10/100/960 h). Gains from 100 h to 960 h are small, and degradation is sharp below 100 h. HuBERT and TERA are said to show similar trends, with no values given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In speech SSL, repeating limited data cannot substitute for unique data at fixed compute, with diminishing returns above ~100 hours.

fits_no_version.finding: At equal parameters (~20M) and compute, a 12-layer narrow Slim model beats a 3-layer Small model on nearly all SUPERB tasks for all three objectives. Example: HuBERT ASR WER 14.56 vs 19.37 (Table 2). Exceptions include TERA SD (10.09 vs 8.53) and wav2vec 2.0 SID (40.46 vs 43.81).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small speech SSL models, depth/width shape substantially changes downstream performance at fixed parameter count (contrast with V4, but different system and measure).

record.problems: The model-size results are presented as plots without numeric values or reported uncertainty. The compute-optimal allocation is assessed at one FLOPS budget, and the data-size table presents detailed results only for wav2vec 2.0 Slim; HuBERT and TERA are described as having similar trends without their table values shown.
record.rows_left_out: None. Table 2 architecture comparisons were not recorded as claim rows because they report downstream metrics, not held-out pretraining loss. Table 3 is recorded for all reported data-size conditions and downstream metrics.

untested.parts: Only one FLOPS budget is used, so it cannot test whether the optimal parameter or token count grows as a stable power of compute. The system is speech SSL, not a language model.
Speech is another modality, but no power-law fit of loss against parameters, data or compute is reported. The data sweep varies repetition at fixed compute and reports downstream metrics only.
No exponents are fitted and no fitting choices are varied. The U-shaped isoFLOP curve is not a departure from a power law.

missing.what: Table 2 Slim vs Small architecture comparison at equal parameters and compute across all SUPERB tasks and three objectives (e.g. HuBERT ASR 14.56 vs 19.37).
missing.versions: none (fits_no_version; related to V4 but speech and downstream)

missing.what: Table 5: Slim at 200% size vs Small at the same compute (e.g. TERA ASR 13.97 vs 19.43; HuBERT ASV 6.60 vs 8.82).

record.verdict_notes: I reject the reader's V3, V6 and V7 labels. V3 'supports' rests on a single budget, which cannot test a power-of-compute trend. V6 rows concern speech SSL, not language models. V7 'supports' misreads a U-shaped isoFLOP curve, which is expected under compute-optimal theory, as a departure from a power law. The study cites Hoffmann et al. only for its FLOPS computation, and cites [30] for an approximate speech power law without testing it. If the project treats speech SSL as in scope for V6 (downstream tracks pretraining loss), F_*_ASR/ASV could be relinked; the evidence is qualitative, figure only, with no correlation statistic. No uncertainty is reported anywhere.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fits of held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute are reported; the model-size sweep holds compute fixed.
No small-run fits or predictions of much larger runs are reported.

The paper tests model-size allocation at one fixed FLOPS budget in speech models. It does not vary compute budgets to establish a stable power-of-compute trend, test token-count growth against compute, or compare parameter and token exponents.
The architecture comparisons report downstream task metrics rather than loss at fixed parameter count.
The study uses speech models but does not test whether the same power-law form holds in speech or other modalities and training regimes.

The paper reports downstream ASR and ASV trends against model size and pretraining loss, and downstream metrics against data size. It does not test downstream-task predictability across other modalities or regimes.

The study shows U-shaped training/validation-loss curves over model size at one compute budget. It does not test how fitted exponents depend on parameter counting, fitting method, training schedule, or data, nor explain disagreements between published laws.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: HuBERT, wav2vec 2.0, and TERA at 1.33 × 10^18 FLOPS
reader_labels.reason: For each tested objective the paper reports an efficient model size near 200% of Slim, based on the fixed-budget sweep (F_HUB_VALID, F_W2V_VALID, F_TERA_VALID). This supports a one-budget optimum, not a power-of-compute trend.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Three model objectives across the fixed-compute model-size sweeps; wav2vec 2.0 Slim across data sizes on most reported tasks
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports similar trends for pretraining loss, ASV, and ASR, and most Table 3 metrics improve as data size increases (F_HUB_ASR, F_HUB_ASV, F_W2V_ASR, F_W2V_ASV, F_TERA_ASR, F_TERA_ASV; D_ASR_10, D_ASR_100, D_ASR_960, D_PR_10, D_PR_100, D_PR_960, D_ASV_10, D_ASV_100, D_ASV_960, D_SD_10, D_SD_100, D_SD_960, D_SFCER_10, D_SFCER_100, D_SFCER_960, D_KS_10, D_KS_100, D_KS_960, D_IC_10, D_IC_100, D_IC_960, D_SID_10, D_SID_100, D_SID_960).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: wav2vec 2.0 Slim at 960 hours for slot filling F1 and emotion recognition accuracy
reader_labels.reason: These metrics dip slightly from their 100-hour values rather than improving monotonically with data size (D_SFF1_960, D_ER_960).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: HuBERT, wav2vec 2.0, and TERA model-size sweeps at the tested fixed compute budget
reader_labels.reason: The text describes U-shaped performance curves, and the validation-loss plots show a model-size optimum rather than a single monotone power-law trend in this fixed-compute setting (F_HUB_VALID, F_W2V_VALID, F_TERA_VALID).
